name: SAS triangle
seoDesc: SAS triangle: work out side c from the side b and the angle γ. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: side c is what the SAS triangle calculator works out, and it gets there from the side b and the angle γ. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the SAS triangle calculator work?
sections.html:
The SAS triangle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side c in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the side b and the angle γ.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the SAS triangle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side c=(the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))
Area=((1 ÷ 2) × side a × side b × the sine of (angle γ))
Perimeter=(side a + side b + (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2))))
Angle α=the smaller of ((side a × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))), (side b × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))))
Angle β=(-angle γ − the smaller of ((side a × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))), (side b × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2))))) + PI)
Angle β=the smaller of ((side a × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))), (side b × the sine of (angle γ) ÷ (the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The SAS triangle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the side b and the angle γ — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the SAS triangle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side c, derived from the side b and the angle γ. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the SAS triangle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side b and the angle γ, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side a in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side a opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: Is the SAS triangle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
